The African National Congress. South Africa's oldest and most influential liberation organization, founded in nineteen twelve to combat racial discrimination and defend Black political rights. Initially pursuing constitutional reform through petitions and negotiation, the ANC evolved into a revolutionary movement under apartheid, employing armed resistance and civil disobedience.

The organization was founded in nineteen twelve with the goal of seeking reform through constitutional means—using petitions and lobbying for voting rights and equitable political representation for Black South Africans. Under apartheid rule from nineteen forty-eight to nineteen ninety-four, the ANC was systematically banned and driven underground. They adopted armed struggle alongside nonviolent resistance and civil disobedience tactics.

Nelson Mandela joined in the nineteen forties and became the ANC's most iconic leader. His imprisonment from nineteen sixty-two to nineteen ninety made him a global symbol of anti-apartheid resistance. A turning point came with the Sharpeville Massacre in nineteen sixty, when police killed sixty-nine unarmed anti-pass law protesters. This radicalized the ANC leadership and convinced them that armed resistance was strategically necessary. They established Umkhonto we Sizwe—Spear of the Nation—as their armed wing to conduct sabotage and military operations.

International sanctions, internal resistance, and economic pressure gradually weakened the apartheid government's ability to sustain the system. Negotiations between the ANC and the National Party government from nineteen ninety to nineteen ninety-four led to Mandela's release, multiracial elections, and a new constitution. After leading the struggle against institutionalized racism, the ANC governed South Africa post-nineteen ninety-four, transforming from opposition force to governing party. Their transition from liberation movement to governing party parallels similar patterns in post-colonial Africa and presents ongoing challenges of governance and accountability.
